newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Opposition slams Bangaldesh water deal with India.
newsitem.headline: Opposition slams Bangaldesh water deal with India.

text.p: Bangladesh's main opposition party on Saturday denounced last week's water sharing treaty with India, saying it served only to protect Indian interests.

"It is an inequitable agreement. The government has sold out the national interest by agreeing to the deal," Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) Secretary General Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan told a news conference in Dhaka.

Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Indian Prime Minister Deve Gowda signed the 30-year Ganges water sharing treaty in New Delhi on Thursday, ending a decades-old dispute between the two South Asian neighbours.
The dispute, which soured the bilateral relations, had emerged since India built the Farakka barrage in 1974, a dam that curbed the flow of the Ganges.
The BNP leader warned his party would mobilise public opinion against the deal and wage movement.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Friday the agreement would be placed before parliament for ratification.
The BNP, which lost to Sheikh Hasina's Awami League in June's elections, has boycotted parliament since November in protest against alleged police repression of its workers.
Bhuiyan said the earlier water agreement in 1977 had been more beneficial for Bangladesh than the current one.
"We would get less water than under the 1977 accord. There is no guarantee this time that we will be getting 35,000 cusecs (cubic feet per second) of water," Bhuiyan said.

Under the 1977 agreement, Bangladesh was guranteed a minimum flow of 34,500 cubic feet water per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But there was no guarantee for a minimum quantum of water in the following six-year accord signed in 1982.
The last water sharing agreement between Dhaka and Delhi expired in 1988 and attempts to renew it had since failed.

The BNP Secretary General criticised the ruling Awami League for not consulting with the opposition prior to signing of the agreement. "It's a national issue...the government should have sought opinion from all."
Under the new deal, if the flow at the barrage is below 70,000 cusecs, both countries would split the the water evenly.

If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will receive 35,000 cusecs and India the rest. If the flow exceeds 75,000 cusecs, 40,000 cusecs would be guranteed to India and Bangladesh the rest.
The fundamentalist Jamaat-e-Islami party also rejected the agreement, saying it was unequal. "Indian diplomacy has outwitted the Bangladesh government," Jamaat said in a statement on Friday.
The Jatiya Party of former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad congratulated the government on Thursday for what it said ensuring highest quantum of Ganges flow since 1975.
The leftist Workers Party termed the agreement "a big success of the democratic and non-communal" forces in both India and Bangladesh.
